svg.title: Issue 001 City Beat Page 2
svg.desc: Fog-season fictional-world local reporting with weather, transit, calendar, and neighborhood notes.
svg.text: CITY BEAT / PAGE 2
CITY BEAT
PORTLAND ABOVE / PORTLAND BELOW / REPORTED BY THE NEIGHBORHOOD
WHEN THE FOG MOVES IN,
THE BLOCK LISTENS
On the working waterfront and in the passages below it, shorter sightlines make ordinary
sounds carry more of the load. Neighbors agree on caution. They do not always agree on what
they heard. The fog came in low enough to erase the end of a wharf before the first coffee
had cooled. Aboveground, chains knocked against metal posts and a ferry horn arrived from
somewhere beyond the white. Below, the same weather pressed cool air through service
corridors and made every drip, cart wheel, and closing door sound nearer than it was. "You
stop measuring distance with your eyes," said a waterfront hand who asked to be identified
only as M. "One bell is the corner. Two is somebody moving a load. Three means put your
shoulder against the wall and let them pass." M. called that an old habit, not an official
code, and said different crews count differently. A night delivery rider who uses both
street and below-street routes disputed the idea that sound becomes clearer. "Louder is not
clearer," the rider said. "A pipe carries a tap three blocks and drops the cart beside you.
I listen for rhythm, but I still wait at a blind turn." The rider said a hand lamp held low
shows feet and wheels sooner than a lamp raised at eye level. A repair steward at the green-
lamp community room recommended the same practice, while warning that pooled water can throw
the light back and make an empty passage look busy. The steward, who gave the name June but
declined a surname, has placed three temporary bell cords at the neighborhood approaches
maintained by volunteers. June described them as a courtesy measure for this fog spell, not
a permanent route system. "If you hear a bell, answer once and wait," June said. "If you
hear scraping, do not guess what it is. Let it come to the light." Not every sound has a
useful explanation. Two residents reported quick steps near a locked waterfront service
entrance after midnight. One believed there were four people; the other heard "maybe two,
moving badly." Neither saw faces. The reports resemble details on Page One, but they do not
establish that a single group-or the rumored "Foot Clan"-was present. The newsroom has not
confirmed that name. For the length of the fog spell, the practical advice is smaller than
the rumors: slow down at blind corners, keep lamps below the line of sight, answer a
neighborhood bell once, and give carts the wall side. Write down what happened before
deciding what it meant. Fog carries sound. It does not carry certainty.
WEATHER DESK
Desk outlook for the fictional Issue 001
neighborhood: dense harbor fog through the
first work rounds, thinning unevenly later;
light drizzle on exposed walks. Fog may
erase the far end of the block before
breakfast. Use bells, lamps, and patience.
This is in-universe reporting, not a real
Portland forecast.
TRANSIT WATCH
GREEN-LAMP APPROACH - WEATHER / COURTESY.
Volunteer stewards report reduced sightlines
through the next two work rounds. Handcarts
should enter one at a time, sound the
hanging bell once, and yield the wall side
to anyone carrying a load. Step-free passage
remains open by the long ramp; expect a
short wait. EAST CART RUN - DELAY. The first
below-street delivery loop is running one
bell-cycle behind while crews walk loads
through the fog. Riders may leave parcels at
the staffed press drop instead. The delay is
an Issue 001 condition, not permanent
geography.
COMMUNITY CALENDAR
SATURDAY, TWO BELLS AFTER NOON - FOG-SAFETY TALK. Green-lamp community
room; organized by the volunteer repair table. Step-free via the long
ramp. Lamps and questions welcome; no registration. SUNDAY, FIRST
AFTERNOON BELL - STORM-DRAIN CLEANUP. Meet at the fictional Harbor
Steps notice board. Gloves and tools provided. Street-level tasks and
seated sorting available. TUESDAY, EARLY EVENING - LANTERN REPAIR
HOUR. Press drop workbench; hosted by June and the repair table. Low
work surface available. Bring a lamp only if it can be safely carried.
THURSDAY, SEVEN BELLS - LOCAL HISTORY LISTENING HOUR. Green-lamp
community room. Memories are welcomed as memories, not filed as
settled history. Quiet seating and step-free access via the long ramp.
NEIGHBORHOOD NOTES
LATCH TABLE. Volunteer repair crews checked eleven shop latches and found
three that needed a second screw. Owners were shown the repair before it was
made. No fee; donations of usable hardware accepted. BEFORE THE CITY IS
READY. The first customers at Tony's Donuts arrived with fog on their coats
and no agreement about whether the ferry horn sounded early. The shop
confirms only that the coffee was on. No special, price, or hour is implied
by this report. RETURNED. A produce crate missing from the press drop
reappeared beside the long ramp, empty, dry, and carrying a note that read,
"WRONG TURN." Nobody has claimed the handwriting. The desk is treating it as
a found item, not a threat.
WE'RE ALL LOOKING FOR A PLACE TO LAND.
THE UNDERGROUND PRESS / ISSUE 001 / CITY BEAT / PAGE 2
